projects.title: Knowledge Factory (LangChain): the knowledge loop that makes business agents improve
projects.what: An article by Harrison Chase (LangChain CEO) describing how all their internal agents (GTM, content, LangSmith Engine) learn continuously. Put simply: permanent onboarding for your agents, like a company wiki that updates itself.
projects.how: Reconstructed from the tweet and the many summaries relayed (the article itself could not be read from the session). 1) Write down what is in your best people's heads: processes as skills (step-by-step procedure sheets the agent loads when needed), how the business works in one linked wiki, and where the data lives and how to access it (tools = functions the agent can call). 2) Agents flag what is missing or wrong while they work. 3) A curator agent goes through those flags and the traces (the detailed log of what the agent did) every night and fixes the source; it is the only agent that edits the wiki, because task agents edit it badly. 4) Skill changes often need human sign-off (HITL, human-in-the-loop); other memory can be merged automatically. Result: agents improve without touching model weights; the wiki is what you diff, review and roll back, like code.
projects.who: Anyone trying to get agents to do real work in a company. The message: the model is rarely the problem, the agent just does not know how your company works. Many field reports in the RTs: Palm built one because different sources gave different values for the same fact; a team applies it to voice agents (knowledge gaps bubble up, humans answer by reviewing the call); another says background agents already make up 20 to 50% of their runs.
projects.try: Free: it is a pattern, not a product. Version 0: a folder of Markdown files (processes, glossary, where the data lives) plus an instruction to your agent: at the end of each task, list what you were missing.

projects.title: Amp Puck in the car: drive your coding agent by voice
projects.what: Amp (Sourcegraph's coding agent, a cousin of Claude Code / Codex) adds a car mode: you talk to your agent, it answers by voice and only shows a big picture or a button now and then. Put simply: a Siri for your coding agent.
projects.how: Puck is Amp's voice assistant. Quinn Slack (CEO) also trained a local wake-word model ("Hey Puck", like "Hey Siri"): Amp generated synthetic data, used 77.2 hours of his own dictation recordings (no one else's data) and wrote native Swift/Kotlin/Web implementations. Local means the model runs on your device, so nothing is sent to the server until you say the keyword (low latency plus privacy). He plans to queue things you need to look at and show them at a red light. Amp already shows up in CarPlay as a call.
projects.who: Shows where agent interfaces are heading: less screen, more asynchronous delegation. Also a nice case of an agent building its own ML component end to end.
projects.try: Available in Amp (paid, pay-as-you-go); the wake word is coming soon. Site not reachable from the session, limited details.

projects.title: Vistara: read your agents' reasons instead of their code
projects.what: A free Mac app, relayed by Harrison Chase, to follow why your coding agents changed something, not just what they changed.
projects.how: Based on the tweet only: the idea is to make the reasoning and intent behind each change readable, because agents write more code than you can read. The exact mechanism could not be checked.
projects.who: Vibe coders who do not read every diff but want to know what changed and why.
projects.try: Free on Mac. Site not reachable from the session, limited details.

projects.title: InstantRecord: Rails models that run in the browser
projects.what: A Ruby gem by Kieran Klaassen (Every) that compiles your Rails app to WebAssembly (a format that runs non-JavaScript code in the browser): your database lives in SQLite in the tab, syncs with the server and works offline (local-first). Demo: 10,601 conversations, first row in about 820 ms.
projects.how: ActiveRecord models are compiled to wasm with the same Ruby code and validations, run on SQLite in the browser and sync with the Rails server.
projects.who: Very technical and not about agents: skip unless curious.
projects.try: Ruby gem; license not verified. Site not reachable from the session, limited details.
